newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK government limits help for future leader Tung.
newsitem.headline: HK government limits help for future leader Tung.

text.p: Hong Kong's colonial government said on Monday it would set limits on how much it would help leader-designate Tung Chee-hwa form a government-in-waiting before the colony reverts to Chinese rule next year.

Secretary for Constitutional Affairs Nicholas Ng told the Legislative Council the government had ruled out any major secondment of high-ranking officials to the future government being assembled by Tung in the coming weeks.

The Hong Kong government rejected any secondment on a major scale because it would negatively affect the civil service, Ng said. Whatever secondments were made would not be allowed to undermine stability and efficiency.

Britain will hand Hong Kong back to China at midnight on June 30 next year, and the colonial administration is supposed to cooperate with the incoming government of the Chinese "Special Administrative Region" under the handover agreement.
But the transition has been fraught with disputes over issues ranging from human rights and democracy to infrastructure projects, darkening prospects for serious cooperation.
"Our position is clear that we should not become victims of the political row between the two governments," the South China Morning Post on Monday quoted a senior official as saying.
"As senior civil servants, we just implement policies. What's wrong with that?" the official said.
Tung, a former shipping magnate, greeted Ng's remarks on Monday as a sign that cooperation of some sort was in the pipeline.
"I welcome any sort of cooperation from the Hong Kong government. But as for the details, I will start working on them after I am formally appointed," he told reporters.
Asked when he would fly to Beijing to be invested by Chinese President Jiang Zemin, Tung said it would be this week, but gave no exact date.
"I think sometime this week. Maybe tomorrow, maybe Wednesday or Thursday. I should soon know," he said.
Tung was chosen last week to step into Governor Chris Patten's shoes by the 400-member, Beijing-controlled Selection Committee.
The chief executive-designate was set to meet senior Hong Kong officials later at a business community dinner party.

Chief Secretary Anson Chan, who is Patten's deputy, and Financial Secretary Donald Tsang were among the other guests he was likely to meet at the gathering. Tung has said he would like Chan to stay in her post.
"I am very happy to know Mr Tung has confidence in me. I very much hope he will make a decision on the rest of his team as soon as possible," Chan said on Sunday.
"It would be a very good thing if all existing principal officials could carry on with their work after 1997," she said.
Tung said he had not yet thought about the composition of his team that will govern the territory after the 1997 handover.
Asked whether he would give assurances to officials about their prospects after 1997, he sidestepped the question and said he looked forward to meeting them.
Local politicians and academics last weekend urged Tung not to bring back former or retired officials to work in his team.

"Former officials are former officials, as they have already left the government. I don't think they should go back in as there is also new talent in the civil service," said Liberal Party legislator Selina Chow.
